# `git status`, `git log`, `git diff`

After this page you can read the three-tree report, walk history, and see a patch before you commit it.

## `git status` — where you are

```bash
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git status
git status -sb          # short: branch + one letter per file
```

`-sb` prints `## main` and lines like `M README.md` (modified) or `?? notes.txt` (untracked). Use it when the long form is noise.

`git status` is the three-tree report from chapter 1: working tree vs index vs HEAD.

```text
 git diff              git diff --staged         git log
 working vs index      index vs HEAD             HEAD chain

 working tree          index                     HEAD
 ┌──────────┐         ┌──────────┐              A ← B ← C  main
 │ extra    │         │ staged   │
 └──────────┘         └──────────┘
```

## `git log` — the DAG as a list

```bash
git log
git log --oneline
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
git log -3                          # last three
git log --oneline -- README.md      # commits that touched this path
git log -p -1                       # last commit plus its patch
```

`--oneline` is the default view in this book. `--graph --decorate --all` is the view that matches the mental-model diagrams.

Useful format:

```bash
git log --format='%h %an %s'
```

`%h` short hash, `%an` author name, `%s` subject. `git help log` lists more placeholders. You will use `--format` in hooks and CI later; for now, `--oneline` is enough.

## `git diff` — the patch

```bash
git diff                 # working tree vs index (unstaged)
git diff --staged        # index vs HEAD (what the next commit will contain)
git diff HEAD            # working tree vs HEAD (staged and unstaged together)
git diff HEAD~1 HEAD     # last commit vs its parent
git diff main feature    # two branches (once you have them, chapter 8)
```

Empty `git diff` and non-empty `git diff --staged` means everything is already in the index. Empty both, plus an untracked file in `status`, means you still need `git add`.

## DiffTool

For a side-by-side view in the terminal:

```bash
git config --global diff.tool nvimdiff    # or vimdiff, meld
git difftool README.md
git difftool --staged
```

`difftool` opens each changed file in the tool you named. `mergetool` is the sibling for conflicts (chapter 8). Stay on `git diff` until you want the split view. The patch is the same data.

## A one-minute drill

```bash
echo "note" >> README.md
git status
git diff
git add README.md
git diff                 # empty
git diff --staged        # the note
git restore --staged README.md
git restore README.md    # discard the note
git status               # clean
```

`restore` is the next page, on purpose. Here you only need to *see* the three diffs change as the file moves.
